Therefore, joining `ITM` with the already distinct `ITPV` set will not introduce any new duplicates for the `(ITEMN, VENDN)` pairs. The final `SELECT` in Q1 does not have a `DISTINCT` keyword, but because of the `ITM.ITEMN` primary key constraint, the result will inherently be a set of unique `(ITEMN, VENDN)` pairs.

Q2 performs a three-way join between `ITM`, `ITP`, and `PUR`, applies all filtering conditions (`ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM`, `ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN`, `PUR.ODATE > 85`, `ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20`), and then applies a `DISTINCT` clause to the final projected `(ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN)` pairs. This also results in a set of unique `(ITEMN, VENDN)` pairs.

Both queries effectively compute the set of `(ITEMN, VENDN)` pairs where an item (from `ITM`) is linked to a vendor (from `PUR`) via a purchase order (in `ITP`), the purchase order date is greater than 85, and the item number is between 2 and 19 (exclusive). The primary key constraint on `ITM.ITEMN` ensures that the `ITM` table does not introduce any row multiplication that would cause Q1 to produce duplicates where Q2 would not (or vice-versa) for the selected columns. Thus, the final sets of `(ITEMN, VENDN)` pairs produced by both queries will always be identical.
